paragraphs.heading: A wave that runs upriver
paragraphs.text: A tidal bore happens when the front edge of the incoming tide forms a wave, or a set of waves, that travels up a river or narrow bay. It pushes against the current and turns the water's direction around. A bore only forms while the tide is rising, never while it is falling. The word goes back through Old English to the Old Norse bára, meaning wave or swell.

paragraphs.heading: Where bores form
paragraphs.text: Bores are found in relatively few places. They usually need a large tidal range, typically more than 6 meters between high and low tide, and a broad bay that funnels the incoming tide into a shallow, narrowing river or lake. That funnel shape raises the range further. It can also squeeze the rising tide into so short a time that the water level seems to jump up all at once.

paragraphs.heading: Different shapes
paragraphs.text: Some bores are a single breaking wave front with a roller, a bit like a hydraulic jump. Others, called undular bores, have a smooth front with a string of secondary waves behind it, known as whelps.

paragraphs.heading: Churning water and a deep roar
paragraphs.text: A passing bore stirs the water violently, and that mixing can reach far along the estuary. Measurements show the flow slowing sharply as the bore goes by, with large swings in speed. Bores also roar: the sound mixes turbulence, air bubbles trapped in the roller, sediment torn from the bed and banks, and impacts on obstacles. Its low notes carry over long distances, so the rumble is heard far away, and the bubbles caught in large eddies do most of the work of making it.

paragraphs.heading: Danger on the water
paragraphs.text: Large bores can be dangerous for ships, and they disrupt boat traffic in estuaries in places such as Papua New Guinea, Malaysia and India. On China's Qiantang River, people die every year by taking too many risks with the bore, despite warning signs on the banks. On Indonesia's Kampar River, locals fear the bore known as Bono for sinking ships.

paragraphs.heading: Food for fish, waves for surfers
paragraphs.text: Estuaries with bores are also rich places for wildlife to feed and breed. Native fish spawn there, and the air the bore churns into the water helps fish and shrimp thrive, for example in Indonesia's Rokan River. Bores draw surfers too, such as on the Seven Ghosts bore of the Kampar River and the Severn Bore in England.

paragraphs.heading: Lost and found
paragraphs.text: People can destroy a bore. The Seine in France had a large one, called la barre, until the 1960s, but dredging and river works have all but removed it. Canada's Petitcodiac River once had North America's highest bore, over 2 metres, until a causeway built in the 1960s caused heavy silting that shrank it to a ripple. Its gates were opened on April 14, 2010, the bore began to grow back, and in July 2013 surfers rode a 1 metre wave 29 kilometres upriver to Moncton, a North American record.
